tasks.task_description: Model the effect of self-driving, cooperating cars on traffic flow for four Washington State highway corridors (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520), answering: (1) how do effects change as AV share goes from 10% to 50% to 90%; (2) do equilibria exist; (3) is there a tipping point where performance changes markedly; (4) under what conditions should lanes be dedicated to AVs; (5) what other policy changes are suggested.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) Peak-hour demand is a fixed fraction (pf=0.11) of average daily traffic (ADT), standard for urban freeways; (b) human free-flow capacity is 2200 pc/h/lane (upper bound of the 1800-2200 range from expert exchange 1); (c) cooperative AVs sustain 1250 veh/h/lane (2.9 s headway, conservative connected-vehicle spacing); (d) the capacity drop is abrupt and hysteretic, not gradual — flow holds near capacity until a critical density, then collapses to 70% of capacity (dd0=0.70) for all-human traffic; (e) latent demand: congested corridors suppress 10% of trips (f_latent=0.10, midpoint of the 5-20% range from expert exchange 2), and half of this returns if capacity is relieved; (f) dedicated-lane operation adds a 15% capacity bonus (b_ded=0.15, modeling assumption); (g) the analysis uses a single peak-hour snapshot per segment, so daily variation is not captured. Method: per-segment capacity model with three regimes (free, hold, break), where the hold regime is an unstable equilibrium representing the hysteresis described by the expert. Throughput is the sum of segment flows; delay is a BPR-type function of V/C. The model is appropriate because it captures the discontinuous capacity-drop structure identified by the expert and the induced-demand offset from exchange 2.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: p = AV share in (0,1); L = number of lanes; ADT = average daily traffic (veh/day); d = 1 if dedicated-lane, else 0. Equations: (1) Base peak demand: D0 = pf * ADT, where pf = 0.11. (2) Capacity per lane: c_lane(p) = (1-p)*c_human + p*c_platoon, where c_human = 2200 veh/h/lane, c_platoon = 1250 veh/h/lane. (3) Corridor capacity: C = c_lane(p) * L * (1 + b_ded*d), where b_ded = 0.15. (4) Latent-demand adjustment: D = D0 * (1 + 0.5*f_latent) if D0 >= 0.9*C, else D = D0, where f_latent = 0.10. (5) Volume-capacity ratio: vc = D / C. (6) Breakdown flow: F = dd(p) * C, where dd(p) = dd0 + (1-dd0)*p and dd0 = 0.70. (7) Regime classification: if D < 0.9*C then regime = 'free', flow = D, delay = 1 + 0.5*vc^2; elif D <= F then regime = 'hold', flow = D, delay = min(4, 1 + 2*(vc-1)^2 + 0.5*vc); else regime = 'break', flow = F, delay = min(4, 1 + 2*(vc-1)^2 + 0.5*vc). (8) Corridor throughput: T(p) = sum(flow) over all segments. (9) Tipping point: smallest p where n_break = 0 and n_hold = 0 (all segments free). Parameter table: c_human = 2200, interval [1800, 2200], source: expert exchange 1 (reply_1); c_platoon = 1250, interval [1000, 1500], source: doi:10.1109/isms.2014.123 (safe following distance ~1-3 s for connected vehicles; 2.9 s headway used as conservative midpoint); pf = 0.11, interval [0.09, 0.12], source: doi:10.3141/2553-13 (peak-hour factor at freeway segments); f_latent = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.20], source: expert exchange 2 (reply_2); dd0 = 0.70, interval [0.60, 0.80], source: expert exchange 1 (reply_1, flow drops to 40-60% of capacity); b_ded = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: modeling assumption (no direct source; sensitivity checked); vff = 55 mph, interval [50, 60], source: doi:10.1007/978-3-319-05786-6_7 (basic freeway segment free-flow speed).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (standard mixed traffic, p = AV share): At p=0, all four corridors are severely over capacity in peak hour: I-5 V/C=2.38, I-405 V/C=2.72, SR-520 V/C=1.85, I-90 V/C=1.68. 100% of I-5, I-405, and SR-520 segments are in the 'break' regime (capacity drop active); 89% of I-90 segments are in break. As p increases from 0 to 1.0, total corridor throughput DECREASES monotonically: I-5 from 716,100 to 581,250 veh/h (-18.8%), I-405 from 198,770 to 161,250 (-18.9%), SR-520 from 46,200 to 37,500 (-18.8%), I-90 from 117,370 to 96,430 (-17.8%). This counterintuitive result occurs because c_platoon (1250) < c_human (2200): adding AVs to the mix reduces per-lane capacity, and the corridors are so over capacity that any capacity reduction translates directly into lower throughput. No tipping point exists: n_break never reaches 0 for any p in [0, 1] for any corridor. Equilibria: the 'hold' regime (unstable equilibrium) never activates because all segments are deep in the 'break' regime; the corridors are far beyond the capacity-drop threshold. Dedicated-lane operation: with b_ded=0.15, dedicated lanes increase capacity by 15%, but the corridors remain over capacity at all p values. Throughput with dedicated lanes is higher than mixed traffic at the same p (e.g., I-5 at p=0.1: 821,723 vs 714,542 veh/h, +15%), but still below the p=0 baseline. Policy implications: (1) AV deployment in mixed traffic REDUCES throughput on these severely over-capacity corridors; it should not be deployed as a capacity solution. (2) Dedicated lanes are preferable to mixed operation if AVs are to be deployed, as they preserve the capacity of the remaining human-driven lanes. (3) The dominant policy lever is demand management (congestion pricing, transit, travel-time shifting) to bring V/C below 0.9, after which AV reliability benefits (reduced breakdown frequency, lower travel-time variability) can be realized. (4) The model's reliability metric (reduced breakdown events) is not achievable on these corridors at any AV share because they are permanently in the capacity-drop regime; the expert's success criterion (fewer breakdowns) cannot be met without first reducing demand. Limitations: (a) single peak-hour snapshot; daily and weekly variation not captured; (b) c_platoon = 1250 is conservative; if AVs achieve 2 s headway (1800 veh/h/lane), the throughput penalty is reduced but the over-capacity problem persists; (c) latent-demand recovery (0.5*f_latent) is a simplification; actual induced demand depends on parallel-route availability; (d) the model assumes uniform AV distribution across lanes; in practice, AVs may cluster in specific lanes, creating non-uniform effects; (e) no interaction modeling of AV-human merging behavior, which can cause additional capacity loss in mixed traffic; (f) the 2200 pc/h/lane capacity is for ideal conditions; real-world capacity is typically 15-20% lower due to grade, curvature, and access points, which would make the over-capacity problem even more severe.
